glosses: Hortative of go, particularly as a cheer expressing encouragement.

examples.text: Let's go to the beach next Saturday.
Let's go, team! C'mon!

glosses: Let us begin or get started. (a call to put a plan into action)
Hurry up; be quick.

examples.text: Let's go, practice starts in five minutes.

glosses: Bring it on. (an incitement to fight)

examples.text: You think you're so tough, huh? Let's go then!

glosses: Yay. (an expression of pleasure, joy, relief, or satisfaction)

examples.text: Our team is up two points already, let's go!

translations.source_sense_description: Teil einer Aufforderung, etwas zu tun

glosses: To encounter, discover; to come upon.

examples.text: Turning the corner, I came on Julia sitting by the riverbank.

glosses: To appear on a stage or in a performance.

examples.text: I think he's coming on too late after my line.

glosses: To be broadcast (through a device), or (of a broadcast) to begin playing.

examples.text: I was going to turn off the TV, but my favorite show came on.
A salsa song came on the radio.

glosses: To progress, to develop; to come along.

examples.text: The new garden is coming on nicely.
But she looked a lady, Paul declared, as much as Mrs. Major Moreton, and far, far nicer. The family was coming on. Only Morel remained unchanged, or rather, lapsed slowly.

glosses: To activate; to turn on.

examples.text: The light came on as soon as I flicked the switch.
She pressed the power button and waited for the screen to come on.

glosses: To show sexual or relational interest through words or sometimes actions.

examples.text: She started coming on to me as soon as my wife left the room.
Wait a minute. Are you like coming on to me? Is this a pass? Because, I mean, if it is, sex is like totally out of the question.
And so you went with Neve / Oh yeah, and Neve was coming on

glosses: To get one's period, start menstruating.

examples.text: Overall, menstrual modernity in the form of a more efficient throwaway technology was seized on and celebrated, as was the opportunity to send your man off to the shop to get it if you came on suddenly.

glosses: To enter the playing field.

examples.text: Blackburn made their third and final substitution with 25 minutes remaining, with Brett Emerton coming on for Dunn as they looked for ways to stem the Newcastle tide.

One of few positives from a Burnley perspective was a first appearance of the season for forward Michael Obafemi, who came on with five minutes remaining after recovering from a long-term hamstring injury

glosses: Elaboration of come (in the sense of move towards the speaker or other focus), emphasising motion or progress, or conveying a nuance of familiarity or encouragement.

examples.text: Don't just stand there on the doorstep. Come on in!
Don't leave without coming on round to see the baby.
You told me to come on over whenever I get the chance, and here I am!
Come on up to my place on the third floor.
Please come on home.

glosses: To appear or seem to be a particular.

examples.text: They came a trick on me.
He's coming on strong.

glosses: To begin to feel the effects of a drug; to start causing effects.

examples.text: The coke came on me quickly.

glosses: To join a job, hobby or other practice.

examples.text: He came on at the same time as me.

glosses: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see come, on.

examples.text: I'll show you where the auditorium is. Come on!

glosses: Synonym of let's go, a cheer or expression of support, encouragement, &c.

examples.text: Come on, George! You can win!

glosses: An expression of disbelief.

examples.text: Come on! You can't possibly expect me to believe that.

glosses: An expression of frustration, exasperation, or impatience; hurry up.

examples.text: Aw, come on! Get on with it!

glosses: An expression of defiance or as a challenge; approach; come at me.

examples.text:

COX: No, sir.
BOX: No? Then come on—
Come on! I'm not afraid of you.
